vignette: He experiences the Tuesday afternoon in vivid detail: the way the gym floor tilts beneath his sneakers, the metallic taste of blood in his throat, then nothing. When he wakes, it is to the rhythmic hiss of a machine breathing for him, the sterile blue of an ICU ceiling, and his parents’ silent, tear-streaked faces pressed against the glass. He has acute myocarditis complicated by cardiac arrest. For three weeks, his body barely obeys him. Doctors speak in measured tones about ejection fractions and vasopressors. He learns to float between awareness and sedation, listening to the steady beep of monitors that sometimes stretch into long, terrifying silences. The discharge comes sooner than expected, but the quiet of his bedroom feels heavier than the hospital wards. He stops watching sports on television. The word “chest” makes his breath catch. He lies awake at 2 a.m., pulse checking his wrist, counting heartbeats like a metronome, waiting for the rhythm to skip. His girlfriend, Clara, notices the way he tenses when the phone rings, how he flinches at the sound of his car’s door slamming shut. He pushes her away gently, telling her he just needs space to “normalize,” but what he really means is that he does not want her to see him unravel. He starts volunteering at a community youth center as a peer counselor, drawn to the work because talking to teenagers feels safer than talking to himself. The center’s quiet office becomes his anchor, but also his mirror. At nineteen, he sits across from students who carry their own heavy histories. He guides them through grounding exercises, teaches them how to name their emotions, and listens without judgment. The work always felt like a lifeline. Now, it feels like a tightrope. When a sixteen-year-old boy describes his heart “fluttering like a trapped bird,” his throat closes. He swallows hard, adjusts his posture, and keeps speaking, but his hands grow cold and his vision tunnels. After sessions, he needs ten minutes alone in his car before he can drive home. He avoids the hospital pharmacy on Main Street, rerouting four miles out of his way because the sharp smell of antiseptic triggers a sudden, breathless panic that leaves him gripping the steering wheel until his knuckles whiten. He stops taking his own prescribed magnesium pills because the small paper cup reminds him of medication carts. He begins arriving at the center an hour early, straightening pamphlets and wiping down chairs, chasing order in a world that suddenly feels unpredictable. Clara notices the distance creeping into his eyes during movies. She reaches for his hand, but he pulls back, telling himself he is protecting her from his own fragility. They argue in hushed tones about trust and exhaustion, but he keeps showing up, keeps listening, keeps pretending the ground beneath him is steady. He and his parents, both from Lyon, try to maintain a household routine. They cook dinner together, but he tastes nothing until the flavors are sharp enough to break through the static. He sleeps with a weighted blanket and a white noise machine, convinced that any sudden silence will signal another collapse. Weekends are for long walks, but he stays on familiar routes, eyes scanning the horizon for emergency vehicles. He tells himself he is healing. He tells his supervisor he is doing well. But when a summer storm rolls in now, the first crack of lightning sends him to the bathroom floor, knees pulled to his chest, whispering “I’m still here, I’m still here” until the shaking stops. He is nineteen. He is learning to live inside a body that once tried to leave him. And every day, he chooses to stay.
